pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 5–6 (UK Y1–Y2, US Grade 2). Using ARRAYS (rows and columns) to represent both multiplication and division — the canonical model that carries commutativity, the ×÷ inverse, and later the area model.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y1 'calculating the answer using … arrays with the support of the teacher'; Y2 'solve problems … using materials, arrays, repeated addition …'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.OA.4 'use addition to find the total number of objects arranged in rectangular arrays with up to 5 rows and up to 5 columns; write an equation to express the total as a sum of equal addends'; feeds 3.OA.1/3.
• Operational details: an array is a rectangle of objects in equal rows and columns. Read it two ways (3 rows of 4 = 4 columns of 3) to see COMMUTATIVITY; read it as repeated addition (each row is a group); cover part to see DIVISION (total ÷ rows = columns). The array is the single most reusable representation in the domain — it becomes the area model for written multiplication.
• Checkpoint: build and read arrays. Tier A (5): make a 2×3 array and count the total. Tier B (5–6): write the multiplication for an array (3 rows of 4 = 12) and rotate it. Tier C (6): from one array write two multiplications and a division (3×4=12, 4×3=12, 12÷4=3).
bestPractices: Build arrays physically in equal rows and columns and describe them precisely as 'rows of' and 'columns of' before recording — the regular structure is what makes the total computable without counting every object.
Rotate the array a quarter turn to reveal commutativity concretely: 3 rows of 4 becomes 4 rows of 3, same total — the array makes 3×4=4×3 obvious rather than asserted.
Read the SAME array as repeated addition (row by row) and as multiplication, so the array ties the two together.
Use the array to introduce division as the inverse: cover the total and ask 'if 12 objects make 3 equal rows, how many in each row?' — one picture yields the whole fact family.
Treat the array as the seed of the area model — keep rows/columns aligned in a rectangle so the later transition to area and the grid/expanded written methods is continuous.
keyRepresentations: The rectangular array of counters/dots (rows × columns)
The array rotated 90° to show commutativity
Fact-family link: one array → two × facts + two ÷ facts
The array as precursor to the area model / grid method for written multiplication
commonMisconceptions: Confusing rows with columns and so mis-describing the array (though the total is the same, the language matters for later).
Counting every object one-by-one instead of using the row/column structure (missing the point of the array).
Not seeing that a rotated array has the same total — treating 3×4 and 4×3 as needing separate counts.
Building arrays with unequal rows (ragged rectangles) — breaking the equal-groups structure.
Not recognising the array as a division picture as well as a multiplication one.

learn.summary: For ages 5–6 (roughly UK Year 1 into early Year 2; US Kindergarten–Grade 1, noting that US standards formally introduce arrays in Grade 2, ages 7–8), use rectangular arrays (equal rows and columns) as a central model for multiplication and division. Learners build arrays, read them two ways to see commutativity, read them as repeated addition, and cover part to reveal division — so one picture yields a whole fact family and seeds the later area model.

activities.title: Build and read an array
feedback: If a learner counts all 12 by ones, model skip-counting each row aloud ('4, 8, 12') and point to each row as you go; the structural view develops with repeated exposure to equal grouping, so do not drill it.
If rows are different lengths (a ragged arrangement), line up the columns and check every row has the same number before reading it — only then is it a true array.
Prompt: 'How could you count the total quickly using the rows?'
activities.rationale: Describing arrays precisely as 'rows of' and 'columns of' before recording makes the regular structure explicit, which is what lets the total be computed from the factors rather than counted individually. If using physical counters, note the counters sit in a flat grid: the array represents a 2D arrangement.
sourceClaims: Y1 use arrays (with teacher support); Y2 solve problems using materials, arrays and repeated addition.
2.OA.4 find the total of objects in rectangular arrays (up to 5×5) and express as a sum of equal addends.
The array is the key representation linking repeated addition, commutativity and the inverse relationship, and is the precursor to the area model for formal multiplication.
learnerActions: Lay out counters (or draw dots) in equal rows and columns to make an array, e.g. 3 rows of 4.
Say aloud exactly what you made: '3 rows of 4' — then also read it as columns: '4 columns of 3'.
Find the total WITHOUT counting every object: skip-count each row, '4, 8, 12'.
Write the multiplication the array shows: 3 × 4 = 12.
Try building another array to order as an extension, e.g. 'Show me 2 × 5 as an array', and state its total.
activities.intendedInsight: An array has a regular row/column structure, so you can find the total by using the rows rather than counting every object one by one.

activities.title: Rotate the array to see commutativity
feedback: If a learner re-counts from scratch after rotating and is surprised the total matches, revisit that the same counters were only turned, none added or removed.
If a learner treats 3×4 and 4×3 as needing separate counts, have them physically rotate the same array rather than build a new one.
Prompt: 'If I turned the array on its side, what multiplication would it show then?'
activities.rationale: Physically rotating one array a quarter turn demonstrates commutativity concretely rather than asserting it, because the same objects are rearranged and the total is preserved. In a screen model this can be an interactive rotate control with the product shown updating live; on paper, physically turning the layout serves the same purpose.
sourceClaims: The array is the key representation linking repeated addition, commutativity and the inverse relationship, and is the precursor to the area model for formal multiplication.
learnerActions: Build 3 rows of 4 and record the total (12).
Turn the whole array a quarter turn so it becomes 4 rows of 3.
Count or check the total again and notice it is still 12.
Write both multiplications from the one array: 3 × 4 = 12 and 4 × 3 = 12.
activities.intendedInsight: Rotating an array turns 3 rows of 4 into 4 rows of 3 while the total stays the same — so 3 × 4 = 4 × 3 is something you can see, not just a rule to remember.

activities.title: Find the division in the same array
feedback: If a learner builds rows of 4 but can't name a division, point to each 'group of 4', count the groups, and name that as 12 ÷ 4 = 3 — bridging both operations on one array.
Prompt: 'What division does your rows-of-4 array show?'
activities.rationale: Using the array to introduce division as the inverse — covering the array, stating the total and the number of rows, and asking how many are in each row — lets a single picture yield the whole fact family, linking multiplication and division. A cover action (physical card or an interactive mask) makes the 'unknown' concrete.
sourceClaims: Y1 use arrays (with teacher support); Y2 solve problems using materials, arrays and repeated addition.
The array is the key representation linking repeated addition, commutativity and the inverse relationship, and is the precursor to the area model for formal multiplication.
learnerActions: Start from a total, e.g. 12 loose counters.
Arrange them into an array with rows of 4; count how many rows you made.
State the division the array shows: 12 ÷ 4 = 3 (12 grouped into rows of 4 makes 3 rows).
Cover the array, tell a partner the total (12) and the number of rows (3), and ask how many are in each row (12 ÷ 3 = 4); then uncover to check.
activities.intendedInsight: One array is a division picture as well as a multiplication picture: the rows and columns are the two factors, and reading the total the other way reveals the inverse fact.

activities.title: Write the whole fact family from one array
feedback: If a learner writes only one multiplication, have them rotate (or re-read) the array to find the second.
If the division facts are missing, link each factor to a dimension: 'how many rows?' and 'how many in each row?'

A tap-to-reveal reference array (callouts for rows, columns, total and the facts) can support learners as a check — but reading and writing the facts themselves, not just recognising them, is the goal.
activities.rationale: Reading the SAME array as repeated addition and as multiplication, and deriving both × and ÷ facts, connects the representations so one picture supports the whole fact family and keeps the rows/columns aligned for the later area/grid method.
sourceClaims: The array is the key representation linking repeated addition, commutativity and the inverse relationship, and is the precursor to the area model for formal multiplication.
learnerActions: Look at a single array (e.g. 3 rows of 4).
Also write the array as repeated addition, row by row: 4 + 4 + 4 = 12.
activities.intendedInsight: A single array ties together repeated addition, two multiplication facts and two division facts — it is a key, highly reusable representation, and the same rectangle later becomes the area model for written multiplication.

constraints: Keep rows and columns equal and aligned in a rectangle; ragged arrangements break the equal-groups structure the array depends on.

Learners should construct and build arrays (from counters, drawing, or a drag-to-set builder), not only recognise or match pre-made ones — recognition/matching tasks check array-reading but do not elicit independent construction.
Keep the rows/columns aligned as a rectangle so the transition to the area model and grid/expanded written methods stays continuous.

Checkpoint tiers: Tier A (age 5) make a 2×3 array and count the total; Tier B (5–6) write the multiplication for an array and rotate it; Tier C (6) from one array write two multiplications and a division.

A static labelled array (e.g. a fixed on-screen image) is a useful reference and can show the fact family, but the learner cannot resize or rebuild it, and a fixed screen image cannot be rotated. Pair it with building/rotating work when the commutativity-by-rotation insight is the aim.

An array is a flat 2D rectangular arrangement; distinguish the grid from any physical counters used to build it. A 3D rendering is not required for this 2D objective and adds handling cost — this is a design judgement for this task, not a claim that 3D provides no learning value in general.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source rated a 'conversation/dialogue' artefact as poor-fit on the grounds it 'adds little' and 3D as adding 'no insight'; these are catalog fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws. They have been softened throughout to scoped notes about the 2D representation and the value of construction; comparative efficacy of any medium is not asserted.

The original pedagogy called the array 'the single most reusable representation in the domain'; this superlative exceeds the cited source claims (which say 'key representation') and has been reduced to a sourced 'key, highly reusable representation' framing.
Source worked examples use 3 rows of 4 = 12 (3×4=12, 4×3=12, 12÷4=3, 12÷3=4) and 2×3=6; arithmetic checked and correct.
Source marks CCSS-M 2.OA.4 and the NCETM claim as verified:false; treat those citations as unverified. The DfE NC claim is marked verified:true in the source but has not been re-checked here.

sourceClaims in Activity 1 attach the DfE and CCSS-M curriculum claims (building arrays with materials; equal-addend/repeated-addition basis) alongside the NCETM structural claim; the NCETM claim most directly supports the precise-structure rationale, while DfE/CCSS support the array-and-repeated-addition basis rather than the specific language principle.

probeDeeper: How could you count the total quickly using the rows?
What division does your rows-of-4 array show?
If I turned the array on its side, what multiplication would it show then?
assess.correctAnswer: The array shows 3 × 4 = 12 (3 rows of 4). Arranging 12 into rows of 4 makes 3 rows — that same picture shows 12 ÷ 4 = 3. The rows and columns match the two factors.

errorPatterns.pattern: doesn't use the array structure — counts every counter one at a time instead of rows × per-row
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT drill — model skip-counting each row ('4, 8, 12'); the structural view of arrays develops with repeated exposure to equal grouping
errorPatterns.revealedBy: counts all 12 by ones with no use of the rows

errorPatterns.pattern: builds a non-rectangular arrangement — makes rows of different lengths so it isn't a true array
errorPatterns.nextMove: align the columns and check every row has the same number before reading it

errorPatterns.pattern: can't read the division from the array — reads 3 × 4 but doesn't see 12 ÷ 4 = 3 in the same picture
errorPatterns.nextMove: point to the 'groups of 4', count the groups, and name that as 12 ÷ 4 — bridging both operations on one array
errorPatterns.revealedBy: builds rows of 4 but can't state the number of rows as a division

responseLevels.gap: Miscounts arrays by counting one-by-one and cannot build an equal-rows arrangement; rows/columns aren't linked to the factors.
responseLevels.full: Reads an array as a multiplication and total, builds an array to match a grouping/division situation, and connects the same array to both operations.
responseLevels.partial: Reads or builds an array for multiplication but doesn't connect it to the matching division, or needs support to keep the rows equal.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is an array — 3 rows with 4 counters in each row. Tell me a multiplication this array shows and what the total is. Now here are 12 loose counters — arrange them into an array with rows of 4, and tell me how many rows you made.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who reads arrays maps rows-and-columns to the factors and the total, both when reading a given array and when building one from a situation. A child without it counts one-by-one (missing the row structure and often mis-totalling), says only 'lots' rather than 3×4, or builds a ragged arrangement with unequal rows. Requiring both an INTERPRET (read the array) and a TRANSLATE (build from a grouping) exposes exactly where the mapping breaks.
